Give the AI one long, complete brief first: the product, the customer, the problem, the features and their benefits.

Then improve the result with several short follow-up messages. Do not start over each time.
Check every AI output for facts and claims before you publish it.

Write the core copy yourself. Use AI as a helper, not as the final writer.
Keep your reference files in one project, so every new chat starts with the same facts.

Copy the **prompts in the code blocks** exactly, and fill in only the [brackets].
**Check every AI output** before you use it. AI can be wrong or invent facts.

Never add numbers, reviews, expert names or customer quotes that you do not have.
Before every ad launch, **turn off Meta's automatic AI changes**.
**Check every AI text and image yourself** before you use it. AI (a computer helper that writes or draws) makes mistakes, and a spell checker does not check if something is true.

**Never publish a claim you cannot prove.**
**Give the AI your brand, your customer and your product facts.** Vague input gives generic output.

**Expect several rounds.** Change one specific thing at a time.
**Test** AI images quickly, then send the winners to your designers for polished versions.
**Check** every word in an AI-made image before you publish it, because AI often gets text wrong.
**Write** all numbers as words before you make audio, because the voice tool mispronounces digits in most languages.

**Keep** the scene prompt plain and add the photo style as a separate step.
**Use** a face-forward portrait for any character that must speak.
Have a knowledgeable person check every AI script and text for false facts before you publish it. This matters most for health, religious and other sensitive topics.
Choose the main message (the angle) first. Then let the AI write the script around it.
Check every image, infographic and subtitle yourself. AI makes mistakes in text, faces and small details.
Test every AI text against real sales results before you spend more money on it.
Tools and project setup
**Claude Projects** (Claude or ChatGPT) keep a knowledge base. A knowledge base is a set of files the AI can read.

It is "persistent" because it stays saved across chats.
**Upload** your reference files once.
Every new chat in the project then reads them automatically.
When you run **Step 9 and Step 10** of the Source D ad workflow, open a new chat inside the project for each angle you test. An angle is the main reason you give the buyer to click or buy.

A new chat keeps the logic of each angle separate.
The project still reads all five reference files.
**Ad Manage.ai** can save ad copy templates. A template is a reusable set of ad text.
A template can hold the primary text (the main text of the ad), the headlines, the description, the call-to-action button (the button that tells people what to do)

and the URL parameters (extra text added to a web address).
URL parameters can include UTM tracking, which are tags that show where a click came from.

**Create** a template from an existing ad.
Or write custom copy.
Or import copy from another ad set (a group of ads with the same settings).

Or paste a URL.
**Load** a saved template into new campaigns (full ad pushes) to keep your message consistent across launches.

The **Inspiration Library** shows competitor ads (ads from rival brands) across platforms.
**Search** it by brand name or keyword.
**Clone** an ad, meaning make a copy of it, and have Claude regenerate it as a custom version.
Set your brand colours, fonts, product name, logo and creative brief (a short written plan for the ad).
The system adapts the design and messaging to your brand identity.
**Canva's AI Magic Media** (an image tool inside Canva, a design app) generates product images.

These images do not exist in real life and carry no supplier logos or brand names.
**Describe** the product in a text prompt (a written instruction to the AI).
**Use** it for demo products or when stock images (ready-made photos) are unavailable.
**Shopify Email** (the email tool built into Shopify, an online store platform) has a built-in **Generate Text** feature.
Tools and project setup (continued)

It creates subject line alternatives (the title line of an email) and email body copy (the main text).
**Choose** the tone: playful, formal or professional.
**Use** it to improve abandoned checkout messages (emails sent to shoppers who left before paying), while keeping brand consistency (the same look and voice everywhere).

**Voice Control for ChatGPT** is a Chrome extension (a small add-on for the Chrome browser).
**Hold the spacebar** and speak to dictate prompts.
It saves a lot of typing when you write long, detailed prompts.
Before you ask an AI tool for ad copy (the written words of an ad), know the product's **desire**,

meaning what the buyer wants to reach or escape.
Know the product's **features** (what the product is or has).
Know the **benefits** (what each feature gives the customer).

Know the target **persona** (a made-up picture of your typical buyer).
Know the **problem** the product solves.

The AI only amplifies the inputs it gets.
**Weak inputs** produce weak copy.
Copy made without product inputs comes out **generic**, meaning vague and able to fit any product.

**Always** give the AI the unique selling points (USPs, the things that make your product different).
Give it the target audience.

Give it the framework (a set structure for the ad).
Do this **before** you ask for headlines (the big top line of an ad) or scripts (the spoken words of a video).
Generic AI copy written without knowing the target audience stays generic.
Give the model the audience, the problem, the market position (where you stand against rivals) and the unique features **first**.

**Check every output** for accuracy before you publish it.
A general chatbot, such as ChatGPT (an AI chat tool), used to write ad copy usually gives weak results.
This is true when it has no best-practice training (proven rules for good ads) or explicit instructions.
Teams that skip this training often decide AI does not work and go back to human copywriters (people paid to write ads).

**Write** detailed instructions and best-practice rules first.
Then **judge** the output.
Keep **one brief** in a spreadsheet (a table in a program like Excel).
Briefing the AI before prompting (continued)
The brief holds the desire, features and benefits, persona, awareness stages (how much the buyer knows about the problem and the solutions),
sophistication stages (how many similar claims the buyer has already heard) and principles (proven persuasion rules).
All of these feed the headline and the body copy (the main text under the headline).
With the brief kept up to date, you can generate Facebook ad copy, landing page copy (text on the page buyers arrive at after a click) and video scripts from the same inputs.

Start with **one long, complete brief**.
It covers the product, desire, features and benefits, audience and chosen principles.
Ideally, **dictate** it by voice.

Then refine with a few short corrections.
In a worked example, strong copy took about **five rounds**.
The number of prompts is not the goal.
Use **short prompts** with minimal wording. Refine in several rounds.
In one comparison, a single long voice prompt followed by a few corrections was faster than many separate prompts.
Read this together with the long first brief: the brief comes first, then short corrections.
Ad copy workflows
**Dictate** the product, the problem, the desire, the features and their benefits, and the target audience into the chatbot in one long prompt.

2. **Ask** for three headlines and three body copy texts for the Facebook and Instagram ad.
3. **Check** whether the headline names the problem and hints at the solution.
If the market is crowded, ask for the unique feature to appear in the headline.
4. **Paste** the list of psychological principles (proven persuasion methods) and ask for the copy to be rewritten with the best ones.

5. **Ask** for bullet points and emojis to format the ad.
6. **Refine** in several short follow-up prompts instead of starting over.
Paid-plan ChatGPT workflow
1. **Describe** the product in plain words.
Include its main target audience, the situation the audience struggles with, and its unique features.

2. **Send** the psychological principles, desire, benefits and persona you wrote.
3. **Ask** for three headline examples and body copy.
4. **Review** the output.
Remove generic phrases, for example "experience the magic of".
Tighten the benefit and the unique mechanism (the way the product works to fix the problem).
5. **Give** the market awareness and sophistication stage, together with the competitors' claims.

Then ask for a rewrite that features the unique mechanism in the headline.
6. For paid social ads (ads you pay to show on social media), **ask** for a shorter version.

Include bullet points, a clear call to action, a limited-time offer and fear of missing out (FOMO, the urge not to miss out).
Add emojis if you want them.
7. **Ask** for variations of a headline that use a named principle, for example how to intensify a headline.
Ideation means brainstorming ideas.
I want you to write headline and body copy for a [PRODUCT: product name and what it does]. Main target audience: [PERSONA: demographics, behavior, pains and fears].
Desire the customer wants to reach or escape: [DESIRE]. Unique features and benefits: [FEATURE 1 => BENEFIT 1; FEATURE 2 => BENEFIT 2].
Market awareness stage: [AWARENESS STAGE: unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware or most aware].
Market sophistication stage: [SOPHISTICATION STAGE 1 to 5] with these existing competitor claims: [COMPETITOR CLAIMS].
Give me three headlines that name the unique mechanism and feature a new mechanism or feature in the headline.
Apply these psychological principles where they fit: problem-agitate-solution, curiosity, social proof, authority and presupposition.
Then write body copy that moves from the problem, through the features and their benefits, to a call to action with a limited-time offer and fear of missing out.
Keep the language plain, specific to the persona, and free of vague phrases.
Two-step breakthrough prompt
Breakthrough advertising is a classic method for writing ads that match what buyers already know.
Send step 1 first, then **wait for the confirmation** before you send step 2.
STEP 1 PROMPT (send first, then wait): You are an experienced direct-response copywriter.
I am selling [PRODUCT NAME AND ONE-LINE DESCRIPTION] to [TARGET MARKET, e.g. owners of large dogs who let them onto the bed]. The main problem I want to solve is [MAIN PROBLEM].
The unique features are: 1. [FEATURE 1: what it is and what it does for the customer]. 2. [FEATURE 2: what it is and what it does for the customer].
Write 3 headline examples for a [AD PLATFORM, e.g. Facebook ad] and 3 pieces of body copy using breakthrough advertising best practices.
I will send you psychological principles and my market awareness and sophistication stages next. Do not write any copy until I send them. Confirm that you understand.
STEP 2 PROMPT (send after the confirmation): Here are my market position and principles. Market awareness stage: [STAGE, e.g. solution aware].
Market sophistication stage: [STAGE, e.g. stage three: prospects have heard all the claims]. Psychological principles to use: [PASTE THE PRINCIPLES LIST].
Using this, rewrite the headlines and body copy. Each headline must include the unique feature or mechanism. Give each headline its own body copy.
Format the output for [AD PLATFORM] with bullet points and emojis so it is easy to read. Keep the required elements: [REQUIRED ELEMENTS, e.g. offer, guarantee, call to action].
Act as a direct response copywriter. I am selling [PRODUCT].
Its unique selling points are [USP 1], [USP 2] and [USP 3]. The target audience is [TARGET AUDIENCE, including their main problem and what they have already tried].
The desire the customer wants to achieve is [DESIRE]. The market awareness level is [unaware of the problem / aware of the problem but not the solutions / aware of solutions but not this product].
The market sophistication is [how many similar products the audience has already seen]. For each feature, explain why it is included and the benefit it gives the customer.
Write three Facebook ad headlines and three body copies for them, using principles from Breakthrough Advertising by Eugene Schwartz, and name the principle each headline uses.
Keep the tone of [BRAND TONE]. Do not invent claims, certifications or statistics; if a claim is needed, mark it as [CLAIM TO VERIFY].
Rewrite the chosen ad copy in [LANGUAGE], make it [SHORTER / LONGER], and use emojis [YES / NO].
p.h: Rewrite prompt for the chosen copy

p.t: Keep every claim from the original copy and do not add new claims. Keep the same hook and call to action, and list any change that alters the meaning.
Facebook video script prompt
Write a script for a Facebook video ad that names the problem and then gives the solution, using the problem, agitate, solution framework.
Use this product information: [PRODUCT], [USP 1], [USP 2], [USP 3] and the target audience [TARGET AUDIENCE]. Add authority and social proof, and end with a clear call to action.
Keep the total length to [LENGTH] seconds, with a hook in the first three seconds, then the problem, the agitation, the solution, the proof and the call to action.
Provide the spoken lines and the on-screen text as separate blocks.
Generate Facebook ad copy for a product using the following process.
p.h: Primary text process (one chat per product)

p.t: Input: the product page URL, the ad creative description (the hook, the visual and the angle), and the brand name. Output: 3 headlines and 3 primary texts. Headline 1 (Problem-Aware): a headline about the offer.
Headline 2 (Solution-Aware): a curiosity gap that makes the reader want the mechanism. Headline 3 (Transformation): an identity shift that makes the reader see themselves already using the product.
Primary text V1 (Problem-Aware): open with the reader's pain point, show you understand their struggle, hint at what is possible, create curiosity about the solution, plant a seed of urgency,
end with a soft call to action; tone empathetic, understanding, hopeful.
Primary text V2 (Solution-Aware): acknowledge they have been looking, address why most solutions fail, show what is different about this product, introduce the mechanism, stack proof
and credibility, create urgency, end with a confident call to action; tone knowledgeable, trustworthy, confident.

Primary text V3 (Transformation and offer): paint a picture of life after using the product, show the exact transformation, state the core benefits, show what is included in the offer, make the offer undeniable,
create urgency to act now. Use the current price, original price and discount percentage from the product page, and keep each text short, scannable and free of unsupported claims.

**Run** the ad copy AI prompt in a separate chat for each product.
Paste the product URL and the creative description, then run the prompt.
**Copy** the three primary texts and three headlines into the ad with matching version numbers.
V1 goes with the problem-aware headline. V2 goes with the solution-aware headline. V3 goes with the identity headline.
**Check** line spacing before you publish.

Meta is the company behind Facebook and Instagram.

This prompt sets a stricter layout: 12 words per paragraph and four emoji lines.
**Use** this prompt when you want a fixed structure.
The process prompt above produces three headlines and three primary texts with V1 to V3 labels.

**Use** the process prompt for product pages with full offer details.
**Use** this prompt for quick, high-intent variations (versions aimed at buyers ready to buy).
Act as a direct-response copywriter who focuses on high-converting Meta ads.
Your job: review the product or creative you're given, pinpoint its central marketing angle, and then produce three alternative high-intent primary texts plus three headlines.
Input fields: Brand or product name: [Insert brand or product name here]. Audience notes: [Insert any notes about your audience here, or leave blank so the AI infers them].
Creative attached: [Yes or No; refer to the file name if relevant]. Stage 1 - Creative and avatar review. Write a brief analysis in three sections: 1.
Marketing angle: the hook (the instant visual, emotional, or vanity payoff) and how it naturally moves the reader toward the functional, long-term, or technical advantage of the product. 2.
Avatar: the buyer's core pains and desires, and the precise reason this creative and angle will halt their scrolling. 3.
Awareness level: the single main awareness stage this ad aims at (Unaware, Problem Aware, Solution Aware, Product Aware, or Most Aware). Stage 2 - Primary text.
Produce 3 Meta-compliant primary text variations for the brand or product, each following this exact layout: - Paragraph 1: an arresting hook centered on the main benefit
Meta primary text and headline prompt (alternative format) (continued)

or pain point (12 words at most). - Paragraph 2: a transition linking the hook to the product's distinctive mechanism, quality, or solution (12 words at most). - Benefit stack: exactly 4 standalone lines.

Every line opens with one fitting emoji, followed by a short, punchy benefit written as [Benefit name]. - Paragraph 3: a clear call to action or a closing value proposition that is hard to dispute (12 words at most).
Hard rules: no paragraph may go over 12 words, so count each paragraph's words before you output it. Keep emojis out of the paragraphs; they belong only at the start of the 4 benefit-stack lines.
Do not make any claim the product page fails to back up. Stage 3 - Headlines.
Write 3 headlines: an offer headline aimed at problem-aware readers, a curiosity-gap headline for solution-aware readers,
and an identity-shift headline for readers focused on transformation. Where it fits, use the current price, original price, and discount as displayed on the product page.
Deliver the Stage 1 analysis first, then the three primary text variations, then the three headlines.

p.t: Write me an ad copy for [your event or offer], offering free [what you offer] if you are not happy with the results. Target audience: [who the ad is for, e.g. adults aged 18 to 65 living within 20 km of the business].
Include a headline, a body text of two to three short sentences that makes the benefit clear, and a call to action such as [call to action, e.g. book a free consultation now].

Write in [language] in a friendly, plain tone, and give me two different versions so I can choose the better one.
**Use** AI-written text as a guide for what to say.

Do not paste it word for word.
**Regenerate** (ask for a new version) when the output is weak.
Short-form and caption requests
For ad copy, ask ChatGPT for short two-line ad texts.

Also ask for video captions (the words shown on a video) for Facebook or TikTok ads.
Then **choose** the tone, for example emotional or funny.

**Regenerate** the response when the first result is weak.
Keep **specifying exactly** what you want.
To draft a request in a single prompt, use this template:

To draft ad copy, you can speak or type a request that says you sell [product], its core purpose is [main purpose], your audience is [target audience], and its key features are [feature 1] and [feature 2],
which translate into [benefit 1] and [benefit 2]. Ask for three headlines and three body texts for a Facebook and Instagram ad.

For stronger copy, send a list of psychological principles and ask for a rewrite that uses the most effective ones to sell the product. For presentation, request bullet points and emojis so the ad looks appealing.
**UGC** means user-generated content, videos that look made by ordinary customers.
**Name** the product and use a problem-agitate-solution framework. This means naming the problem, making it feel worse, then showing the fix.

**Refine** the output before you send it to creators or agencies.
**Ask** the AI to rewrite copy in a casual tone.

Or ask it to translate the copy into another language, for example French.
For direct rewrites, this can replace a separate grammar or tone-checking tool.

Before you name a persuasion framework in a prompt, **ask** the AI whether it knows that framework by name.
If it confirms, it can apply the framework directly.

If not, **describe** the framework briefly inside the prompt.
**Refine** iteratively, meaning in repeated rounds.

Treat the AI as an assistant for back-and-forth work, not as a one-shot writer.
The first output is often broad or misses the unique feature.
**Steer** it with specific corrections, such as "this word is too much" or "surface the feature in the headline".
**Ask** for a specific tone of voice or persona, for example a friendly everyday person, a mum, or a target group.
Then have someone from that target group **read the copy** to check whether it sounds authentic (real and believable).
Worked example: pet hair removal brush
Starting point: a pet hair removal brush with a static (fixed, not moving) microfiber head (a soft fabric pad)

and a storage lid.
It is aimed at owners of German shepherds who let their dogs on the bed.

Step 1: the first AI brief produced broad headlines and body copy.
These named the problem but not a unique feature.
Step 2: because the market was solution-aware, the headline was rewritten.
The new headline named the microfiber head as the differentiator (the thing that sets the product apart).
Step 3: a list of persuasion principles was added and the copy was rewritten.
This introduced future pacing (picturing life after the purchase), scarcity (limited supply) and curiosity angles.

Step 4: bullet points and emojis were requested for the Facebook ad format.
Outcome: the copy was much more competitive than the first draft.
It still needed a **human check** for tone and claims.
**AI has changed ad creative** more than any shift since social media took hold.

It lets a team produce ideas, variations and finished assets (ready-to-run ads) much faster.
It gives more variety and far less manual effort.

Using AI to generate ads **without knowing how to direct it** usually produces low-quality ads that perform worse.
The tool alone does not create good creative.

The operator's strategy decides the result.
Brands that keep winning with AI-assisted creative follow a small set of underlying principles.

These principles are not a single tool or prompt trick.
Understanding them lets an advertiser adapt when platforms change their rules.

**Input quality** decides the result of ChatGPT concept work.
A human must **check the output**.
Overreliance makes the work weaker.
So **write the core copy yourself** and check it against customer pain points (the problems customers feel).
**Adjust** copy and creative direction to match your brand voice (the way your brand sounds).
Also adjust it to the customer psychology insights from your research.
Research-first ad creative (Claude Project)
Run this procedure in **one Claude project** named after your product.
1. **Create** a Claude project and name it after your product.
2. **Set up** three prompts as project instructions (standing rules the project follows): Market Research, Emotional Valence Framework, and Target Evidence.

3. For the Market Research prompt, **provide** your website and product information.
Then add information about customer surveys, personas and behaviour data.

More detail produces better output.
4. **Run** the Market Research prompt.

Review the full research document to understand your market.
Add the insights to the project.
5. **Copy and paste** the Emotional Valence Framework prompt into the same project.

Review the analysis thoroughly to understand your customers' psychological drivers (the inner reasons they act).
6. **Copy and paste** the Target Evidence prompt.
Provide your Facebook ad account data (the numbers from your Facebook ads dashboard) from 2 to 3 days of running the product.
Include gender and age breakdowns, spend patterns, top creative themes and geographic concentration.
7. **Ask** Claude to generate bottom-of-funnel ads (ads aimed at people close to buying) using all the research insights you have gathered.
8. **Customise** and refine the generated ads with specific tweaks and details suited to your business.
Product copy, editorials and email
**ChatGPT** (an AI chat tool) can write product descriptions, ad copy, SMS (text messages) and email templates (ready-made text with blanks) in many
languages. If a response is weak, **regenerate** it (ask again for a new answer) instead of accepting the first output.
Template for a product description, ad copy, SMS or email:
Write me [product description / ad copy / SMS / email] for [product], aimed at [target audience, e.g. women above 45 living in Australia].
Write in [language] and use the words and phrases that people in that market use. If the result is not good enough, regenerate it.
Product descriptions (continued)
**Marketing angles** (different reasons a buyer might want the product):
Write 10 different marketing angles for [product, e.g. zodiac jewelry], aimed at [target audience]. For each angle, name the problem it solves, the emotion it targets and a short headline.
**Customer problems** (what your buyers want fixed):
List [number] main problems that [target audience] wants to solve with [product category], ranked by how strongly they feel each problem. Give one short sentence per problem.
**Gary Halbert style** (Gary Halbert was a famous sales writer). Use this prompt:
I'm building my website homepage and you are Gary Halbert, one of the greatest copywriters of all time, and you can sell anything using words. Rewrite me the entire text in Gary Halbert style.
Add the product details, features and benefits after this prompt, and **check the output** before using it.
**Marketing-principles structure:** first give ChatGPT the product, its features, its benefits and its market position (where it stands against others).
Ask for headline copy using problem-agitate-solution (state the problem, make it hurt, then offer the solution).
Then give a list of psychological principles (proven ideas about how people decide to buy) and ask it to use them where they will sell best.
Start the request with an expert role, such as a marketing expert, and **review the output** to make sure it matches your audience.
**Product description with human review** (a person checks the work):
1. **Give** ChatGPT the product name and product URL (the web address of the product page), or supplier information (the company that makes or ships the product).
Also give it a direct-response copywriter role (a writer of sales text that asks the reader to act).
2. **Request** the format: headline, one to three sentences, description, features and benefits, and bullet points.

3. **Fact-check** the output against the product, because AI output is not always accurate.
4. **Tweak** the wording before publishing.
Please act as a direct response copywriter. Please write a product description for [product name] and [product URL].
Use this format: headline, one to three sentences, description, features and benefits, and bullet points. Do research with Bing.
Editorials (70/30 split, AIDA)
An **editorial** is a long, article-style sales page.

The **70/30 split** means 70% of the text tells the story and 30% introduces the product and the action. **AIDA** stands for Attention, Interest, Desire, Action: the four steps a good sales text goes through.
1. **Copy** the text of a proven editorial you want to copy the structure from.
2. **Paste** it into ChatGPT and ask for a response with the same structure, adjusted for your own product.
3. **Describe** your product in detail, including how it is different, its outcomes and its results.
4. **Check** that the output keeps the 70/30 split and the AIDA order, then edit it for accuracy and claims.
You are a direct-response copywriter. Below is a proven editorial page that uses a 70/30 split and AIDA order.
Write a new editorial for my product, [PRODUCT NAME], in the category [PRODUCT CATEGORY], for this ideal customer: [IDEAL CUSTOMER DESCRIPTION]. Keep the same structure: 1.

Headline: benefit-driven, with a bold claim, a curiosity element or a news angle. Give 5 options. 2. Attention and interest: open with a character who fits the ideal customer and tells a story about the problem.
Agitate the problem and explain why it happens. 3. Desire: explain why current solutions on the market fail to work well, then present my product as a new approach.
Let an expert or a satisfied customer recommend it in the story, and do not name the brand early. 4.
Social proof: include one customer result with a timeline (for example after one week and after two weeks), a data point or graph placeholder, and a count of other customers who had good results. 5.
Action: in the final 30% of the text, introduce the product and end with the button text [CALL TO ACTION, e.g. check current availability] linking to [PRODUCT PAGE URL].
Use only the facts I provide here: [PRODUCT FACTS: key features, outcomes, measured results, price]. Do not invent statistics, reviews, expert names or customer quotes.
Mark any missing information as [PLACEHOLDER]. Add a photo placeholder wherever a picture would help the story. End each paragraph with a hook that leads into the next one.
Email and abandoned cart
An **abandoned cart** is a shopper who filled a basket but did not pay.

A **primer** is a setup message that teaches the AI about the brand before you ask for work. A **thread** is one ongoing chat.
Prime the AI before writing abandoned cart text:
1. **Send** the brand questionnaire (a form with questions about the brand) to the client. It takes about an hour to fill in properly.
2. **Paste** the answers into ChatGPT and ask it to learn the brand.
3. **Edit the first message** and restart the thread instead of adding follow-up questions, so the brand instructions are not forgotten.

4. **Run** the email prompt, then the subject line prompt, in the same primed thread.
5. If the output drifts from the branding, **paste the primer prompt again**.
Shopify Email's **Generate Text** feature (a button that writes text for you) is listed under the tools section above for subject lines and body copy.
**Cold outreach** means contacting people who do not know you yet.
Please write me a cold calling email script for my marketing agency for dentists.
ChatGPT produced a usable script in **one attempt**. Use the output as a guideline rather than copying it word for word, and regenerate it if the result is weak.
A **cutoff** is the date after which the AI knows nothing new. Some prompts below mention it.
List 10 blog post ideas for [your store domain].
Use the store's niche and product types in the request if the site was built after the model's cutoff, for example: list 10 blog post ideas for an e-commerce store selling [your product type].
Write 10 short, inspiring social media posts for [your niche] that speak to people who buy [your product type].
Each post should be under 280 characters (about 280 letters and spaces) and suggest one simple action the reader can take.
If the store was built after your model's training cutoff, describe the store in the request rather than using its domain name.
Ebooks and free-gift content
An **ebook** is a digital book. A **free gift** is something you give away to earn trust. An **avatar** is a clear picture of your ideal buyer.
Act as a seasoned ebook writer and content strategist.
Produce a finished, high-grade ebook of 15 to 25 pages to serve as a free giveaway for [TARGET AVATAR: who they are and the problem they have], linked to [PRODUCT NAME],
which assists with [PRODUCT PROBLEM].
Pick a widely applicable, timeless theme suited to this readership, for example productivity, mindset, health routines, personal finance basics, or something similar.
Execution counts for more than the subject: the piece should demonstrate what a well-crafted free-gift ebook looks like in practice.

Deliver the complete ebook from start to finish, containing: - An attention-grabbing title and subtitle - A short welcome note or author introduction - 4 to 6 chapters of substantial, truly practical material,

with no placeholder text - Practical takeaways or exercises wherever they fit - A closing section offering one clear, gentle next step Quality benchmarks: - A warm, direct, engaging voice, never stiff

or generic - Brief paragraphs, subheadings, and bullet points where they improve readability - Each chapter provides genuine value rather than padding - The tone should read like a thoughtful present,
not a sales pitch - The ebook serves as a reference model for others, so its structure, voice, pacing, and the way the content leads into the closing next step should all be polished.
Closing: refer to [PRODUCT NAME] a single time, softly, as support that complements the habits in the ebook, not as a cure or hard sell.
Include a call-to-action link only when one is supplied: [OPTIONAL CALL TO ACTION LINK].

2. **Add** the image in Canva and place a name or text on it.
3. **Write** a script of about 300 words in ChatGPT, telling a short story that teaches something related to the product.

4. **Turn** the script into audio with an AI voice tool.
5. **Combine** the audio with the character image in an AI lip-sync tool so the character appears to speak.
6. The result is a video of about three minutes that you can test as an ad creative (an ad picture or video).
AI UGC video ads for books were produced with Arcads. A second AI video generator is also mentioned, most likely Kling 3.0. **Confirm** the second tool name before relying on it.
Have a knowledgeable person check every script for factual accuracy before you publish it. ChatGPT (an AI chat tool) can write false statements.
This is especially important for religious, health or other sensitive content.
**Write all numbers as words.** Write names and foreign terms the way they sound. This helps the text-to-speech tool (software that reads text out loud) pronounce them correctly.
**Choose the angle first**, the main reason the ad gives for buying, from the research sheet (your notes about the market). Then have the AI draft the script around it.
**Replace the example product** in the brand name prompt (the ready-made instruction text) with your own product.
Then paste the complete brief (all the instructions) in step 2.
**Decisions that need a trained answer** belong in the training, not in the AI's guesses.
Examples are UGC creator placement (where videos made by ordinary customers are used) and hook timing (when the hook, the first few seconds that catch attention, appears).
Quality control and proofing
Checking generated copy and images
**Check every important fact** in the generated copy and brief before you publish. AI tools like ChatGPT can make mistakes.
**Check that the offer** (the deal the customer gets, such as a discount) is visible in the final design.
**Rewrite template copy** (ready-made text) for your brand instead of keeping the defaults, even if you plan to edit it again later.
**Check every word** of a generated infographic (a graphic with text and charts) before you publish it.
**Always check the generated text** for correct offers before you run it.
**Check that every image shows a clearly different model** (the person in the picture). Regenerate any image that repeats a person.
**Check that the output looks realistic** and does not misrepresent the product before you use it in ads or on the store.
**Review and adapt every AI output** for a specific product and region (country or market) before use.
AI subtitles (the words shown on screen that match the speech) make errors on complex or less common words.
The tool is built around basic vocabulary. **Always compare** the generated subtitles with the original script in a second window. Correct each mistake before export (saving the final video file).
**Test every generated text** against real conversion results (how many viewers actually buy) before you scale it,
meaning spend more money on it.
**Check that the output still matches** the brand voice (the way the brand speaks) and the offer after you apply a saved prompt.
**Run a quick test first.** If the test works, send the concept to designers for more variations (versions).
Human control
AI can handle scale (large amounts of work) better than one human.
But **a human must stay in control** and check that the AI learns from the right sources. Oversight is needed for nuance (subtle meaning) and final decisions.
**Use one clean, well-lit product photo** as the source. Blurry or low-quality uploads produce weak variants.
**Spend more time on mask painting** (painting over the parts of an image you want to remove or change) for a clean removal.
Case: AI presenter ads at scale
Starting point: a small brand, Simple Brand, sold a dietary supplement (a product taken by mouth,
such as a vitamin) in the US. Its product showed **strong sales** on Kalodata (a research tool that shows product sales data) in summer 2025.
What was done: the brand ran a large set of ads that were all AI-generated, with different AI presenters (an AI lady, an AI doctor, an AI man).
It launched on **July 9, 2025** and had about **71** active ads (ads still running) in Meta Ad Library (Meta's public list of all running ads) after roughly one month.
The main brand behind the product had about **650** active ads, all AI-generated with avatar variations (versions of a digital presenter).
Result: the ads kept running for about a month. This shows the spend (money put into ads) returned enough money to continue. **The brand scaled the presenter versions that held up.**
Note on conflicting rules: the case shows an AI doctor presenter performing well.
The persona prompt (the instructions for a made-up character) says never to design a medical doctor or any persona that suggests medical qualifications.
The 'Doc Ellie' title example in the same prompt conflicts with that rule. **Follow the prompt rule** for your own personas.

Note on conflicting advice on AI people: real users build trust faster early on. The case scaled AI presenters that held up in tests. **Use real people for early trust** and AI presenter variants for testing and scaling.
Limits of AI output
AI tools like ChatGPT can make mistakes. **Check every important fact** in the generated copy and brief before publishing.
AI tools work as a virtual assistant (a helper that does tasks) rather than as a lead (the main guide). Their output is only as good as the input.
They miss contextual details (background clues) that a human finds in forums and reviews.

**Use an AI tool to draft ad copy** from audience research (what you learned about your buyers). But feed it the right inputs. The quality of the output depends on the quality of the information given.
The AI generates text and images from the prompt (the instruction you type). Unprompted visual or layout suggestions were weak, so **tie image prompts to a specific offer**.
Image generators return the same person when prompts describe models identically. **Describe each model differently.**

AI-generated infographics can contain small text errors.
Generated subtitles make errors on complex or less common words.

ElevenLabs (a text-to-speech voice tool) reads digits correctly **only in English**.
Realistic-looking AI people build less trust than real users early on.

Decisions that need a trained opinion must be defined in the training, not left to the AI.
Generated product visuals must be checked for realistic product representation before use.
A generated text still needs to be tested against real conversion results before it is scaled.
AI-generated ads let you test many presenter types (avatars, which are digital presenters) for the same product at low cost.
